pages.title: Introduction
pages.content:
Introduction

FastAPI is a modern, high-performance Python web framework for building APIs. It is built on top of

Starlette

(for the web

parts) and

Pydantic

(for the data parts), and it takes full advantage of Python type hints to give you automatic data validation,

serialization, and interactive documentation.

Why FastAPI?

Fast

: Performance on par with NodeJS and Go, thanks to Starlette and async support.

Fast to code

: Type hints enable editor autocompletion and fewer bugs.

Automatic docs

: Interactive API documentation (Swagger UI and ReDoc) generated for free.

Standards-based

: Built on open standards like OpenAPI and JSON Schema.

Easy to learn

: Designed to be intuitive, with excellent editor support.

Who This Book Is For

This book assumes you know basic Python (functions, classes, decorators) but does not assume any prior web framework

experience. We progress from installing FastAPI and writing your first endpoint, all the way to authentication, databases,

testing, background tasks, WebSockets, and production deployment.

How This Book Is Organized

The book is divided into four parts:

1.

Part I — Foundations

: environment setup, routing, parameters, and request/response bodies.

2.

Part II — Core Features

: validation, dependency injection, middleware, and error handling.

3.

Part III — Real-World Applications

: authentication, databases, background tasks, WebSockets, file uploads.

4.

Part IV — Advanced & Production

: testing, advanced Pydantic, project structure, deployment, and performance.

Each chapter includes runnable code examples. Type them out yourself rather than copy-pasting — it builds muscle memory.

2.1 HTTP Methods

FastAPI provides a decorator for each HTTP verb:

Each corresponds to a standard CRUD-style operation:

GET

(read),

POST

PUT

(replace),

PATCH

(partial update),

DELETE

(remove).

2.2 Path Parameters

Path parameters are declared using curly braces in the route and typed function arguments:

Because

item_id

is typed as

int

, FastAPI automatically:

Parses and converts the value from the URL string.

Validates that it really is an integer (returns HTTP 422 if not).

Documents it correctly in the OpenAPI schema.

Order Matters

When you have both a fixed path and a parameterized path, declare the fixed one first:

If

/users/{user_id}

came first, a request to

/users/me

would match it and treat

"me"

as a

user_id

.

Chapter 3: Request Bodies and Pydantic Models

3.1 Why Pydantic?

Pydantic models let you declare the “shape” of incoming JSON data using ordinary Python classes and type hints. FastAPI uses

these declarations to validate, parse, and document request bodies automatically.

3.2 Using a Model as a Request Body

FastAPI reads the body as JSON, validates the data against

Item

, converts types as needed (e.g. string

"10.5"

to float), and

gives you a fully-typed Python object — with editor autocompletion.

3.3 Combining Body, Path, and Query Parameters

FastAPI is smart about where each parameter comes from, based on its declaration:

Parameters that match a path segment →

path parameter

.

Singular types (

int

,

str

,

bool

, etc.) →

query parameter

.

Parameters declared as a Pydantic model →

request body

.

3.4 Nested Models

Pydantic handles arbitrarily nested models, lists of models, and dictionaries, validating the whole structure recursively.

Field

Chapter 6: Dependency Injection

6.1 What Is a Dependency?

A

dependency

is a callable (usually a function) that FastAPI runs before your path operation, and whose return value is

injected into your function’s parameters. Dependencies are FastAPI’s mechanism for sharing logic — database sessions,

authentication, pagination, rate-limiting — across many endpoints.

6.2 Class-Based Dependencies

6.3 Sub-Dependencies

Dependencies can themselves depend on other dependencies, and FastAPI resolves the whole graph, caching results within a

single request by default:

6.4 Dependencies with

yield

(Setup / Teardown)

This pattern is the standard way to manage resources like database sessions:

Code after

yield

always runs after the response has been sent (or if an exception occurs), guaranteeing cleanup.

pages.content:
Chapter 10: Async Programming in FastAPI

10.1

def

vs

async def

FastAPI supports both regular and asynchronous path operation functions:

Use

async def

when your function

await

s something (an async database driver,

httpx

async client, etc.).

Use plain

def

for CPU-bound or blocking work — FastAPI automatically runs these in a thread pool so they don’t block the

event loop.

Never

call blocking code (e.g.

time.sleep

, a synchronous DB driver) inside an

async def

function — that blocks the entire

event loop for all concurrent requests.

10.2 Calling External APIs Asynchronously

10.3 Running Concurrent Tasks

For work that should happen

Chapter 12: WebSockets

FastAPI supports WebSockets for real-time, bidirectional communication.

Each connected client keeps an open TCP connection; the server can push messages at any time without the client polling.

fastapi

def

__init__

(

self

self

.active_connections:

list

[WebSocket]

=

[]

def

(

self

, websocket: WebSocket):

websocket.accept()

self

.active_connections.append(websocket)

def

disconnect(

self

, websocket: WebSocket):

self

.active_connections.remove(websocket)

async

def

broadcast(

self

, message:

str

):

for

connection

in

self

.active_connections:

await

connection.send_text(message)

(websocket)

{

{

client_id

16.1 A Scalable Directory Layout

For anything beyond a toy app, split routes, models, and logic into modules using an

└── services/

16.2

APIRouter

16.3 Best Practices Checklist

Keep path operation functions thin; push business logic into a service layer.

Use

response_model

on every endpoint to control your public contract.

Centralize configuration with

pydantic-settings

, never hardcode secrets.

Version your API (e.g.

/api/v1/...

) from day one.

Use dependency injection for anything cross-cutting: auth, DB sessions, rate limits.

Write tests alongside routes, not after the fact.

Log structured JSON in production, not plain

print()

.
